stimulus.source_note: Data table from the U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.
stimulus.text:
| Year | 1959 | 1964 | 1965 | 1966 | 1969 | 1973 |
| Poverty rate | 22.4% | 19.0% | 17.3% | 14.7% | 12.1% | 11.1% |

Official poverty rate, all people. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.

stem: The table best supports which judgment about Johnson's goal of ending poverty?

options.misconception: The rate in 1969 is 12.1 percent, so more than one American in ten was still poor.

options.text: Johnson's programs had no effect on poverty at all
options.misconception: The rate falls steeply from 1964 to 1969, so the claim of no effect does not fit the table.

options.text: Poverty fell sharply but was not ended
Poverty rose again as soon as Johnson left office
options.misconception: The rate falls from 12.1 percent in 1969 to 11.1 percent in 1973, so it did not rise.

rationales.A: The rate in 1969 is 12.1 percent, so poverty was still there for more than one American in ten.
rationales.B: The rate falls from 19.0 percent in 1964 to 12.1 percent in 1969, a steep fall.
rationales.C: The rate falls by more than a third from 1964 to 1969, yet 11.1 percent of Americans were still poor in 1973.
rationales.D: The rate falls from 12.1 percent in 1969 to 11.1 percent in 1973, so it did not rise after Johnson left.
rationales.general:
1. The rate falls from 19.0 percent in 1964 to 12.1 percent in 1969: a sharp fall.
2. A sharp fall is real progress toward Johnson's goal.
3. But the last number in the table is 11.1 percent in 1973, not zero.
4. Poverty therefore fell sharply but was not ended.
Remember: A falling number and a zero are different results.
